title: Issuing in euros and holding euros were two different bets
summary: Christian Noyer saw the euro’s first year as evidence that borrowers could help establish an international currency well before investors treated its securities as one fully integrated market. In the first three quarters of 1999 the euro accounted for 38% of gross international issuance of money-market instruments, bonds and notes, close to the dollar’s 41%. The corresponding share of the euro’s predecessor currencies and the ECU had been 24% a year earlier. The comparison is a flow of new international securities across currencies. It says nothing directly about outstanding portfolios, reserve allocations, net capital inflows or whether issuers kept their exchange-rate exposure. Those distinctions matter for an investor tempted to read the rise in issuance as a directional EUR signal (section 2).

Noyer offered two explanations for the jump. Borrowers could have postponed deals prepared in 1998 until the conversion weekend was past. They also had an incentive to establish liquid benchmarks rapidly in the new denomination. Both would bring issuance forward without a permanent change in the relative cost of funding. Against a purely temporary interpretation, euro issues had continued to grow over the course of the year. His structural explanation was that issuers anticipated a wider investor base, lower dealing costs and more liquid securities. Easier diversification could attract further international users and help deepen domestic markets in turn. The speech advances that feedback as a prospect. The issuance statistics do not identify which incentive drove individual deals.

The strongest contemporaneous evidence of integration was at the very short end. The money market already recorded higher trading volumes and tighter bid–ask spreads at short maturities. Extending that result to corporate credit required several more steps. Banks facing greater competition might securitise more assets or lose business to direct issuance. Large European mergers were creating a need for corporate bond finance. Noyer even saw room for a substantial high-yield segment to emerge. This described how the supply of tradeable credit could expand. It left investors to establish whether marginal issuers were compensating them for default risk and whether secondary trading would remain liquid outside the largest benchmarks.

A common currency also left plenty of room for differences between government bonds. Separate fiscal policies sustained differences in credit and liquidity premia. Equity markets, settlement systems and market conventions were still segmented. A market assembled by adding up all national issues on paper offered less immediate depth in practice. A euro-area investor could therefore gain a common funding and unit-of-account framework yet retain exposure to country-specific credit and settlement risks. These qualifications sit alongside Noyer’s expectation of eventual gains and help explain why the money market provided a better initial demonstration of integration than the securities markets.

The domestic rationale for the currency rested on trade and competition. The eleven economies together represented about 15% of world GDP, compared with 20.5% in the US and 7.8% in Japan. Noyer put their share of world exports at 19.5%, against 15% and 8.5%, respectively. Among individual member countries, average exports and imports as a share of domestic GDP averaged around 30% and exceeded 60% in Belgium and Ireland. These country openness figures and the area’s world export share have different denominators. For countries selling similar goods to each other, exchange-rate shifts could abruptly redistribute margins for reasons unrelated to changes in relative productivity. In highly open economies, depreciation might ultimately raise domestic prices and erode much of an initial competitive gain. Removing internal currency swings was especially valuable in an already integrated single market (section 1).

The hard part was adjusting to shocks after governments surrendered their exchange rates. Noyer regarded sectoral and regional disturbances as particularly important, and saw room for more flexible labour and product markets. Fiscal policy remained national, with medium-term balance or surplus intended to leave room for automatic stabilisers within the Treaty’s 3% deficit limit. Monetary authority lay with a Governing Council whose members had an area-wide responsibility. Noyer thought greater price transparency and competition could themselves encourage structural reforms, bringing the union closer over time to the conditions for sharing a currency. That sequence was conditional on adjustment actually taking place. He distinguished the collective arrangement from unilateral adoption of another country’s currency and from the much more speculative possibility of private electronic settlement displacing central-bank money.

His exchange-rate judgement was favourable. A recovering economy, domestic price stability and a sound current account gave the euro scope to appreciate. He supplied no target, horizon, price already discounted by investors or commitment to intervene. The Eurosystem intended international use to develop through private decisions, subject to its domestic price-stability mandate. Globally, Noyer envisaged greater co-operation among the US, Europe and Japan while rejecting fluctuation bands for their currencies. European representation in international institutions still reflected powers divided among the Eurosystem, national governments and European institutions (section 3).

The same distinction between currency use and institutional integration underlay his discussion of European neighbours and Argentina. Some 34 countries in the wider region had arrangements involving the euro or its legacy currencies, from informal anchoring to baskets and currency boards. For accession countries, evolving trade and institutional links affected the future case for a peg. In Argentina, official dollarisation might deliver a one-off credibility gain, reducing the devaluation component of interest rates and easing pressure from high real borrowing costs. Sovereign credit risk could survive denomination in dollars. Trade links with Brazil, Mercosur and Europe could also make a permanent dollar anchor less suitable than the near-term financing argument suggested. Noyer treated banking-system soundness, openness and existing currency substitution as relevant conditions. He offered neither a forecast of Argentine rates nor a numerical estimate of the saving (section 4).

questions.question: Was issuing in euros persistently cheaper once borrowers hedged the proceeds?
questions.detail: Start with the BIS issuance series cited in the speech and contemporaneous deal records. Separate inaugural benchmarks, postponed deals and repeat issuers. Compare equivalent maturities and credit quality, and reconstruct funding costs after the cross-currency swap. A one-off issue-size effect and a sustained all-in funding advantage imply different prospects for issuance and currency demand.

questions.question: How much liquidity did the common denomination deliver away from the largest benchmarks?
questions.detail: Compare bid–ask spreads, turnover, repo financing and settlement costs for matched benchmark and smaller issues. Separate sovereign from corporate bonds and the money market from longer tenors. The depth available when reducing a position is more relevant for a liquidity trade than the aggregate face value issued.

questions.question: Who retained the euro risk created by new international issues?
questions.detail: Compare investor allocations and positions in the bonds with issuer and investor hedging disclosures where available. International debt issuance alone cannot establish that investors increased net EUR exposure. The answer separates an argument about the franchise of the currency from an argument about its exchange rate.

questions.question: How much of an anchor country’s borrowing spread represented convertible-currency risk?
questions.detail: For the Argentina example compare closely matched dollar and local-currency obligations, taking account of maturity, liquidity and creditor rights. Use contemporaneous central-bank and sovereign-debt publications. Remaining sovereign spread after currency risk is removed affects how much relief a change of regime could plausibly deliver.
